llama_translation: The vulture does not hover over a dry leaf.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb means that everyone has their own unique strengths or resources, even if they are not immediately visible.
claude_interpretation: A powerful or resilient person is not easily destroyed by small threats or minor obstacles.
gemini_interpretation: One should not abandon their inherent nature or identity due to external circumstances or tools.
mistral_interpretation: One's survival or success is not determined by external challenges or limitations beyond one's control
llama_interpretation: One should not waste time or resources on something that is unproductive or has no potential.

yoruba: Ìgbà tí a bá rẹni lòwúrọ̀ ẹni.
english_literal: Whenever one first sees a person, that is that person's morning.
interpretation_gold: One does what one has to do when it is convenient for one to do it.
deepseek_translation: When we borrow someone's morning.
claude_translation: When we carry someone, it becomes that person's morning
gemini_translation: The time when we find someone to use in the morning is ours.
mistral_translation: When one covers oneself in the early morning.
llama_translation: The time we are calling a person a dwarf, the person is growing
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb teaches the importance of gratitude and reciprocity when receiving help or favors from others.
claude_interpretation: When you help or support someone, they benefit from a fresh start or new opportunity.
gemini_interpretation: It is important to seize opportunities when they arise, especially early on.
mistral_interpretation: It warns against taking unnecessary precautions too early, as it may be premature or counterproductive.
llama_interpretation: Do not underestimate someone's potential for growth or progress.

yoruba: Ìgbà tí a bá dóko làárọ̀ ẹni.
english_literal: The time of one's arrival on the farm is one's dawn.
interpretation_gold: People must not be slaves of time but use time to their own advantage.
deepseek_translation: The time we spend on the farm is our morning.
claude_translation: The time when one becomes mature is one's morning
gemini_translation: It is when we get to the farm that we greet our companion.
mistral_translation: It is when we get to the farm that we will weed one's portion.
llama_translation: The time we are pounding yam is not the time to be playing with someone
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb emphasizes that hard work and dedication (symbolized by farming) are the foundation of a successful and fulfilling life.
claude_interpretation: Maturity and wisdom mark the true beginning of a person's meaningful life, regardless of their actual age.
gemini_interpretation: One should address issues or acknowledge people at the appropriate time or place, not prematurely.
mistral_interpretation: One should address their own responsibilities and challenges directly rather than interfering in others' affairs.
llama_interpretation: One should focus on the task at hand and not be distracted by frivolous activities.

yoruba: Ilé ajá là ńwá ìwo lọ?
english_literal: Is a dog's house the place to go in search of horns?
interpretation_gold: One should not bark up wrong trees.
deepseek_translation: Is it in the dog's house we search for the tail?
claude_translation: Is it a dog's house we are looking for you to go to?
gemini_translation: Is it in the dog's house that we look for horns?
mistral_translation: Is it a dog's house that we are going to look for you in?
llama_translation: Is the dog's house where we are going?
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb teaches that one should look for things where they are most likely to be found.
claude_interpretation: This is used to question someone who is being too selective or demanding about accommodations when they should be grateful for what is offered.
gemini_interpretation: It is foolish to search for something in a place where it is inherently impossible to find it.
mistral_interpretation: It is foolish to search for someone in an unlikely or inappropriate place where they would not be found.
llama_interpretation: This proverb cautions against following someone blindly without knowing their true intentions or destination.

yoruba: Igbó lẹranko ńgbé.
english_literal: The forest is the home for animals to live in.
interpretation_gold: Everything in its proper place.
deepseek_translation: The forest is where animals live.
claude_translation: Animals live in the forest.
gemini_translation: The forest is where animals live.
mistral_translation: It is the forest that the wild animal carries.
llama_translation: The forest is where the elephant lives.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb emphasizes that everything has its natural place or habitat.
claude_interpretation: Everyone has their natural place or environment where they belong and thrive best.
gemini_interpretation: One should remain in their natural or appropriate environment to thrive.
mistral_interpretation: One's environment or circumstances significantly influence one's behavior or fate.
llama_interpretation: One must be prepared to face challenges and difficulties in order to achieve greatness.

yoruba: Iná kúkú ni yó ba ọbẹ̀ ará oko jẹ́.
english_literal: It is too much fire that will ruin the stew of a bushman.
interpretation_gold: An ignorant person will ruin whatever venture he/she embarks on with his/her ignorance.
deepseek_translation: It is fire that will destroy the soup of the farmer.
claude_translation: It is fire that will help the soup of the farm person to cook.
gemini_translation: A small fire will spoil the soup of the villagers.
mistral_translation: It is the fierce fire that will spoil the soup of the farmer's wife.
llama_translation: A small fire is what we use to roast the yam of a farmer.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns that one's own actions or negligence can lead to their downfall.
claude_interpretation: Success requires the right tools and conditions, just as cooking requires fire regardless of one's social status.
gemini_interpretation: Even a seemingly insignificant problem can have a detrimental effect on the well-being or efforts of a community.
mistral_interpretation: Excessive anger or harshness can ruin what should be a beneficial or harmonious situation.
llama_interpretation: One should use the resources available to achieve one's goals.

yoruba: Ìjà ní ńpa onítìjú; ogun ní ḿpa alágbára.
english_literal: A street fight is the death of a bashful person; warring is the death of a strong man.
interpretation_gold: One should not rather court danger or disaster simply to avoid losing face.
deepseek_translation: Fighting kills the timid; war kills the brave.
claude_translation: Quarrels kill the shameful person; war kills the strong person.
gemini_translation: Shame kills the shy person; war kills the strong person.
mistral_translation: Shame kills the shy person; war kills the brave one.
llama_translation: Fighting is what kills the warrior; war is what kills the brave.
deepseek_interpretation: Conflict brings harm to all, regardless of their nature or strength.
claude_interpretation: Different types of conflicts affect people according to their nature - minor disputes harm those who are easily embarrassed, while major battles harm even the physically strong.
gemini_interpretation: Different individuals are vulnerable to different challenges or circumstances based on their inherent nature or strengths.
mistral_interpretation: Excessive timidity or reckless boldness can both lead to ruin.
llama_interpretation: Bravery and strength are often tested and sometimes lost in the very challenges that require them.

yoruba: Jùrù-fẹ̀fẹ̀ jùrù-fẹ̀fẹ̀, ewúrẹ́ wọ ilé àpọn jùrù-fẹ̀fẹ̀; kí làpọ́n rí jẹ tí yó kù sílẹ̀ féwúrẹ́?
english_literal: Busily wagging tail, busily wagging tail, a goat enters a bachelor's house busily wagging its tail; what does a bachelor have to eat whose left-over the goat can have?
interpretation_gold: One wastes one's time expecting some largesse from a destitute person.
deepseek_translation: Jùrù-fẹ̀fẹ̀ jùrù-fẹ̀fẹ̀, the goat enters the soap maker's house jùrù-fẹ̀fẹ̀; what will the soap maker do to the goat?
claude_translation: Quietly, quietly, the goat entered the soap maker's house quietly; what will the soap maker find to eat that will be left for the goat?
gemini_translation: Jùrù-fẹ̀fẹ̀ jùrù-fẹ̀fẹ̀, the goat entered the bachelor's house jùrù-fẹ̀fẹ̀; what did the bachelor eat that would be left for the goat?
mistral_translation: Slowly, slowly, the goat entered the soap-maker's house slowly; what will the soap-maker eat if he leaves the goat behind?
llama_translation: The tortoise's shell is hard, the tortoise's shell is hard, the goat enters the tortoise's house; can the goat eat the tortoise's shell?
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb warns against carelessness or arrogance in the face of danger, as the goat foolishly enters the soap maker's domain (where it risks being turned into soap).
claude_interpretation: When someone sneaks into another's livelihood or territory, they shouldn't expect to benefit from what little resources remain.
gemini_interpretation: This proverb questions the expectation of receiving something from someone who has very little themselves.
mistral_interpretation: Patience and persistence can lead to unexpected gains, but carelessness may result in losing what one already has.
llama_interpretation: One cannot harm or destroy what is well-protected or fortified.

yoruba: Kókó ló kọ́kọ́ dé orí, tàbí orí ló kọ́kọ́ dé kókó?
english_literal: Was it the lump that first got to the head, or the head that first got to the lump?
interpretation_gold: A chastisement for someone attempting to reverse the order of precedence.
deepseek_translation: Did the kola nut climb to the head, or did the head climb to the kola nut?
claude_translation: Did the cocoa pod first reach the head, or did the head first reach the cocoa pod?
gemini_translation: Did the knot first arrive on the head, or did the head first arrive on the knot?
mistral_translation: Did the cocoa bring the cocoa to the head, or did the head bring the cocoa to the cocoa?
llama_translation: Is it the head that created the body or the body that created the head?
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb questions the origin of a situation, emphasizing that cause and effect are not always clear.
claude_interpretation: This questions the order of cause and effect, emphasizing that determining what came first or who is responsible can be complex and unclear.
gemini_interpretation: This proverb questions which came first in a complex or intertwined situation, highlighting the difficulty of determining origin or cause.
mistral_interpretation: It questions the origin of a problem or situation, emphasizing the need to identify the root cause before assigning blame.
llama_interpretation: This proverb highlights the interdependence of two entities, suggesting that neither can exist or function without the other.

yoruba: Kí ni à ńwọ̀ nínú-u ṣòkòtò mẹ́ta ọ̀ọ́dúnrún?
english_literal: What is there to wear in a pair of trousers bought at three for three hundred cowries, or three a penny?
interpretation_gold: Much ado about a worthless thing.
deepseek_translation: What are we looking for in three torn trousers?
claude_translation: What are we looking for inside three hundred pairs of trousers?
gemini_translation: What are we looking for in three hundred trousers?
mistral_translation: What are you looking for in a pair of trousers that has lasted thirty years?
llama_translation: What is it that we see in a three-legged stool that is sixteen years old?
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb teaches that one should not waste time on things that are clearly worthless or beyond repair.
claude_interpretation: Some searches or pursuits are excessive and unnecessary when a reasonable amount should suffice.
gemini_interpretation: This proverb questions the futility of searching for something in an excessive and impractical number of places.
mistral_interpretation: It advises against expecting too much from something or someone that has already served its purpose for a long time.
llama_interpretation: This proverb cautions against judging something solely based on its appearance or age.

yoruba: Kéré-kéré leku ńjawọ; díẹ̀-díẹ̀ leèrà ḿbọ́ ìyẹ́.
english_literal: Bit by bit the rat consumes the leather; gently gently the ant sloughs its skin.
interpretation_gold: One should use caution in all one's enterprises.
deepseek_translation: Little by little the bird builds its nest; bit by bit the rat digs its hole.
claude_translation: Little by little the rat eats the beans; bit by bit the ant reaches the salt.
gemini_translation: Little by little the rat gnaws the trap; little by little the termite eats the feather.
mistral_translation: The rat enters quietly in small bits; the bush-rat will eventually be caught in the trap little by little
llama_translation: A small axe is used to cut a small tree; a big axe is used to cut a big tree.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb teaches the value of patience and persistence in achieving goals through gradual effort.
claude_interpretation: Persistence and patience in small, consistent efforts eventually lead to achieving significant goals.
gemini_interpretation: Significant achievements or destruction are often the result of small, consistent efforts over time.
mistral_interpretation: Small, consistent efforts or deceptions will eventually lead to significant consequences or success
llama_interpretation: The tool or approach used should match the size or complexity of the task at hand.

yoruba: Kì í jẹ́ kí etí ẹni di kì í jẹ kí inú ẹni dùn.
english_literal: Whatever keeps one from being deaf to certain things keeps one from being happy.
interpretation_gold: One should learn to turn a deaf ear to certain things for the sake of one's peace of mind.
deepseek_translation: It is not because one's ears are long that makes one's stomach happy.
claude_translation: It should not be that one's ear becomes such that it prevents one's heart from being happy
gemini_translation: It does not allow one's ear to be deaf; it does not allow one's mind to be happy.
mistral_translation: It is not right for one's ear to be unharmed while one's heart is not happy.
llama_translation: What will not make a person's body swell will not make a person's stomach sweet
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb teaches that external appearances or privileges do not guarantee inner satisfaction or fulfillment.
claude_interpretation: One should not let negative things heard through gossip or bad news destroy their inner peace and happiness.
gemini_interpretation: A situation that prevents one from hearing or understanding also prevents one from being content or at peace.
mistral_interpretation: True well-being requires both external peace and inner contentment.
llama_interpretation: One should not expect to enjoy the benefits of something without being willing to endure its challenges.

yoruba: Kì í ṣe gbogbo ẹni tí ńṣe “Ẹni Ọlọ́rún bùn ó bùn mi” là ńfún ní nǹkan.
english_literal: It is not to every person who says “Whoever has received some bounty from God should give to me” that one gives alms.
interpretation_gold: One should be judicious as to those to whom one shows kindness.
deepseek_translation: It is not everyone who says 'God gave you, give me' that we give things to.
claude_translation: It is not everyone who says 'What God blesses, let it bless me' that we give things to.
gemini_translation: It is not everyone who says “God has blessed you, bless me too” that we give things to.
mistral_translation: Not everyone who says 'May God bless me' is given things
llama_translation: It is not everyone who says 'God helps me' that God helps
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns against blindly trusting or giving to those who claim divine entitlement without discernment.
claude_interpretation: Not everyone who speaks piously or makes religious declarations deserves trust or generosity, as actions matter more than words.
gemini_interpretation: One should be discerning about who they help, as not all pleas for assistance are genuine or deserving.
mistral_interpretation: Not all who express good wishes or prayers will receive what they desire; actions and circumstances matter more than words.
llama_interpretation: Not everyone who claims to be devout or righteous is truly favored by the divine.

yoruba: Kóǹkólóyo: èyí tó ní tèmi.
english_literal: A rather small thing: this is enough for me.
interpretation_gold: However small it is “usually a child”, one is glad to have it.
deepseek_translation: Konkoloyo: the one who has mine.
claude_translation: Kóǹkólóyo: this one that says 'mine'
gemini_translation: Kóǹkólóyo: this one is mine.
mistral_translation: The small one: this is the one that belongs to me.
llama_translation: The tortoise: it is the one that has a hard shell.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb emphasizes the importance of recognizing and valuing those who support or possess what belongs to you.
claude_interpretation: It criticizes selfishness and possessiveness, warning against those who claim ownership over everything.
gemini_interpretation: The proverb emphasizes the importance of claiming and taking ownership of one's possessions or responsibilities.
mistral_interpretation: Small or seemingly insignificant things often hold personal value or are uniquely suited to one's needs.
llama_interpretation: One's strength or resilience is often hidden from the outside.

yoruba: Kàkà kí ọmọdé pàgbà láyò, àgbà a fi ọgbọ́n àgbà gbé e.
english_literal: Instead of permitting defeat by a child in a game, an elder should resort to elderly wiles.
interpretation_gold: An elder should protect his face and standing by all means available.
deepseek_translation: Rather than a child growing old in happiness, an elder will use the wisdom of elders to guide them.
claude_translation: Instead of a child rejoicing over an elder, the elder will use elder's wisdom to carry him.
gemini_translation: Instead of a child defeating an elder in a game, the elder will use elder's wisdom to win.
mistral_translation: Instead of a child surpassing an elder in joy, the elder uses the elder's wisdom to support them
llama_translation: When a child's buttocks touches the ground, an elder uses an elder's strength to lift it
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb emphasizes the importance of elders using their wisdom to guide the younger generation, even if it means sacrificing immediate happiness.
claude_interpretation: An elder will use their superior wisdom and experience to overcome any challenge posed by a younger person.
gemini_interpretation: Elders often possess superior wisdom and experience that allows them to overcome challenges, even against younger, more agile opponents.
mistral_interpretation: Elders should guide and uplift the young with their wisdom rather than compete with or resent their success.
llama_interpretation: Community elders have a responsibility to support and uplift younger generations when they stumble or fall.

yoruba: Kò sí ẹni tí kò mọ ọgbọ́n-ọn ká fẹran sẹ́nu ká wá a tì.
english_literal: There is nobody who does not know the trick of putting meat in the mouth and making it disappear.
interpretation_gold: Nobody is a complete fool.
deepseek_translation: There is no one who does not know the taste of salt that will put it in their mouth and then look for it.
claude_translation: There is no one who does not know wisdom that we should love to speak and come to push/press.
gemini_translation: There is no one who does not know the wisdom of putting a fish in one's mouth and then pushing it in.
mistral_translation: There is no one who does not know the taste of bitter cola who would love it at first taste and come to spit it out.
llama_translation: There is no one who does not know the bitter leaf that will love the soup and come to eat it.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb means that people often pretend not to know things they are fully aware of, usually to avoid responsibility or consequences.
claude_interpretation: Everyone possesses some form of wisdom, so we should not be quick to dismiss others or force our own opinions upon them.
gemini_interpretation: It is foolish to pretend ignorance of something obvious or to deny something clearly beneficial.
mistral_interpretation: People often reject things they initially dislike without giving them a fair chance, especially if they are unfamiliar with their true value.
llama_interpretation: One must be aware of the difficulties or challenges involved in a situation before getting involved.

yoruba: Kò sí aláásáà tí ńta ìgbokú; gbogbo wọn ní ńta oyin.
english_literal: There is no snuff seller who will advertise her ware as awful; they all say they are selling honey.
interpretation_gold: Everybody presents himself/herself in the best light.
deepseek_translation: There is no bee that stings the skull; all of them sting the flesh.
claude_translation: There is no prayer leader who sells charcoal; all of them sell honey.
gemini_translation: There is no seller of bitter kola who sells bitter kola; they all sell honey.
mistral_translation: There is no cloth that chases a squirrel; they all chase honey.
llama_translation: There is no type of soap that is not used to wash the body; all of them are used to wash the body.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns that everyone is vulnerable to harm, especially in their weak spots.
claude_interpretation: Religious leaders present themselves as pure and beneficial while avoiding association with anything that might tarnish their reputation.
gemini_interpretation: People often present their offerings or themselves in the most appealing light, even if it means misrepresenting the true nature of what they offer.
mistral_interpretation: People are drawn to what benefits them, not to those who pursue them.
llama_interpretation: Everyone has a role to play in the community, regardless of their background or status.

yoruba: Kí ni ìyá aláṣọ ńtà tó yọ ẹgba lọ́wọ́? Ewúrẹ́ ńjẹ wúlìnì?
english_literal: What is the cloth-selling woman have to sell that she carries a whip in her hand?
interpretation_gold: One should not engage in meaningless or unnecessary activities.
deepseek_translation: What does the mother of the cloth seller who has money have to do with the goat eating the yam peel?
claude_translation: What is the cloth seller's mother selling that she removes twenty from her hand? Is the goat eating velvet?
gemini_translation: What is the cloth seller's mother selling that she is removing a hundred cowries from her hand? Is the goat eating wool?
mistral_translation: What does the mother of the cloth-seller sell that she wraps a hundred (cloths) around her waist? Does the goat eat indigo?
llama_translation: What is the mother of the cloth seller doing, taking the cloth to the market? Is the goat eating the okra?
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns against meddling in affairs that do not concern you.
claude_interpretation: This proverb questions unrealistic or impossible situations, suggesting that some claims or expectations are too far-fetched to be believable.
gemini_interpretation: This proverb questions the logic of an action or situation that seems inherently contradictory or impossible.
mistral_interpretation: It mocks someone who pretends to be wealthy or generous but lacks the means to back it up.
llama_interpretation: This proverb highlights the absurdity of a situation where someone is doing something that is not their responsibility or is unnecessary.

yoruba: Lójú òpè, bí-i kọ́lọgbọ́n dàbí ọ̀lẹ.
english_literal: As far as the dunce is concerned, the wise person should rather be shiftless.
interpretation_gold: The worthless person always wishes others were equally worthless.
deepseek_translation: In the eyes of the ungrateful, a kind person looks like a lazy person.
claude_translation: In the eyes of the palm tree, the one who climbs skillfully appears like a lazy person
gemini_translation: In the eyes of the ignorant, the wise person looks like a lazy person.
mistral_translation: In the presence of the palm tree, it is as if there is no wisdom like that of a lazy person
llama_translation: The eyes of a palm tree, it is not the same as the eyes of a human being
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns that ungrateful people may misinterpret kindness as laziness or weakness.
claude_interpretation: What appears effortless to observers often requires great skill and experience that goes unrecognized.
gemini_interpretation: Those who lack understanding often misinterpret the actions or wisdom of others, perceiving diligence as idleness.
mistral_interpretation: The proverb warns that some people may appear foolish or lazy when compared to the achievements or stature of others.
llama_interpretation: Things are not always as they seem, and appearances can be deceiving.

yoruba: “Màá kó ẹrú, màá kó ẹrù” là ḿbá lọ sógun; ọ̀nà lẹnìkẹta ḿbáni.
english_literal: “I will capture slaves and I will capture loot” is what one has in mind on departure for a war; the third one comes upon one only along the way.
interpretation_gold: Too often one is so preoccupied with the good aspects of a proposition that the bad aspects sneak up on one.
deepseek_translation: “I will carry a slave, I will carry a load” is how I went to war; the third way is what meets me.
claude_translation: I will carry the load, I will carry the burden is what one goes to war with; the third person helps one with the way
gemini_translation: “I will carry the load, I will carry the burden” is what one says when going to war; the road is the third person accompanying one.
mistral_translation: “I will gather loads, I will gather luggage” is what I say when going to war; the third way is what benefits me.
llama_translation: Don't go to the slave's house, don't go to the slave's farm; the path of the lazy leads to the farm of the diligent.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns that overconfidence and lack of preparation can lead to unexpected challenges.
claude_interpretation: Success requires both personal determination to bear responsibility and the guidance or assistance of others who know the path forward.
gemini_interpretation: In times of great challenge or adversity, one must be prepared to face difficulties alone, as external support may be limited.
mistral_interpretation: Overconfidence in one's plans can blind one to better, less obvious solutions.
llama_interpretation: Hard work and diligence are necessary for success, while laziness leads to dependence on others.

yoruba: “Máa jẹ́ ǹṣó” lọ̀yà fi ńju ẹmọ́ lọ.
english_literal: “Go on feeding” is what makes the cane rat fatter than the Tullberg's rat.
interpretation_gold: Excessive consideration for others can be disadvantageous.
deepseek_translation: "Do not be stingy" is what the hawk uses to carry away the chick.
claude_translation: It is 'I will eat the palm nut' that the squirrel uses to chase away the monkey
gemini_translation: “Keep watch for me” is how the lawyer defeats the squirrel.
mistral_translation: It is 'I will dress well' that the toad uses to wash its face
llama_translation: It is the one who will eat that is invited to the farm
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns that excessive generosity or lack of caution can lead to exploitation or loss.
claude_interpretation: Empty threats or boastful claims without action are ineffective ways to intimidate others.
gemini_interpretation: A person who is vigilant and prepared can overcome a seemingly more agile or cunning opponent.
mistral_interpretation: People often make empty promises or excuses to justify their actions or shortcomings.
llama_interpretation: One is only invited to participate in an endeavor if they will benefit from it.

yoruba: Mójú-kúrò nilé ayé gbà; gbogbo ọ̀rọ̀ kọ́ ló ṣéé bínú sí.
english_literal: Judicious forebearance is the wise approach to the world; not every matter deserve to be angry at.
interpretation_gold: The best way to live is to ignore petty annoyances.
deepseek_translation: The eye that leaves home is respected; all words do not fit in the mouth.
claude_translation: Close your eyes is how the world receives; not every word is worth getting angry about.
gemini_translation: To look away is how the world is accepted; not every word is worth getting angry about.
mistral_translation: Do not turn your back on the world; no matter what happens, it is not worth getting angry about.
llama_translation: The eyes that see the world are the ones that take it; all the ears that hear do not know the pain.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb teaches that discretion and knowing when to speak or act are essential for maintaining respect and harmony.
claude_interpretation: Sometimes it's better to overlook things and ignore provocative words rather than react with anger to everything.
gemini_interpretation: It is wise to overlook some things and not react to every provocation in life.
mistral_interpretation: Life’s challenges are inevitable, so one should remain resilient and avoid excessive frustration over things beyond control.
llama_interpretation: One must experience things personally to truly understand their value or challenges.

yoruba: Màjèṣín dóbò àkọ́kọ́, ó sáré yọ okó síta, ó ní Olúwa-á ṣeun.
english_literal: The tender youth has sex for the first time ever, pulls out his penis prematurely, and says “God be praised!”
interpretation_gold: A novice knows not how to relish good things.
deepseek_translation: The squirrel dug a hole for the woodpecker, it ran out to remove the penis, it said thank God.
claude_translation: The inexperienced person fell into the first pit, he quickly pulled out his hoe, and said 'Thank God.'
gemini_translation: Màjèṣín, the first time he saw a vagina, he quickly pulled out his penis and said, 'Lord, thank you.'
mistral_translation: The rider dismounted at the foot of the akoko tree, ran to the farm outside, and said, 'Thank you, God.'
llama_translation: The farmer who planted yams in the forest, he cleared the bush and said God did it.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb warns against deceitful assistance, as the squirrel's help ultimately harms the woodpecker.
claude_interpretation: A novice who encounters their first major difficulty often feels grateful just to escape with their basic tools or dignity intact.
gemini_interpretation: This proverb humorously depicts someone who is overly eager or prematurely excited about something they desire, even before fully understanding or engaging with it.
mistral_interpretation: It teaches that one should express gratitude to God even after overcoming a challenge or achieving success.
llama_interpretation: This proverb highlights the importance of acknowledging one's own effort and not attributing success solely to divine intervention.

yoruba: Ní ìlú tí a ò ti fẹ́ ẹyẹlé, tí a ò fẹ́ adìẹ, irú ẹyẹ wo ní yóò jí wọn lójù orun?
english_literal: In a town that does not tolerate pigeons and does not tolerate chickens, what sort of bird will awaken them from sleep?
interpretation_gold: A person who will not be pleased by anything will simply have to do without everything.
deepseek_translation: In a town where they dislike pigeons, and they dislike chickens, what kind of bird will wake them at dawn?
claude_translation: In a town where we don't want pigeons and we don't want chickens, what kind of bird will wake them up at dawn?
gemini_translation: In a town where pigeons are not wanted, and chickens are not wanted, what kind of bird will wake them from their sleep?
mistral_translation: In a town where we do not want pigeons, nor chickens, what kind of bird will wake them at dawn?
llama_translation: In a town where we have not seen a vulture, where we have not seen a chicken, what kind of bird will come and wake them up from heaven?
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns against rejecting all available options, leaving oneself with no alternatives.
claude_interpretation: If you reject all available options or helpers, you cannot expect to receive any benefits or assistance.
gemini_interpretation: This proverb questions how a community that rejects common and useful things will be alerted to danger or important events.
mistral_interpretation: If you reject all available options, you leave yourself with no solution or help.
llama_interpretation: This proverb cautions against unnecessary interference or meddling in the affairs of others.

yoruba: Nítorí èèyàn la ṣe ńní ọwọ́ ọ̀tún; òsì là bá lò.
english_literal: It is on account of people that one has a right hand; one could do with only a left hand otherwise.
interpretation_gold: One must learn the grace that is appropriate for decent company.
deepseek_translation: Because of people we have the right hand; the left is what we use.
claude_translation: It is because of people that we have the right hand; we would have used the left.
gemini_translation: It is because of people that we have a right hand; otherwise, we would use the left.
mistral_translation: It is because of people that we use the right hand; it is the left we use when alone.
llama_translation: It is because of humans that we have the right hand; the left hand is what we use to help.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb emphasizes the importance of social harmony and adaptability, suggesting that societal norms dictate our actions even when they contradict personal preference.
claude_interpretation: We adapt our behavior and customs to accommodate others and maintain social harmony, even when it means changing our natural preferences.
gemini_interpretation: One must conform to societal norms and expectations, even if they seem arbitrary, to maintain social harmony and acceptance.
mistral_interpretation: People adjust their behavior based on social expectations or the presence of others.
llama_interpretation: One should use their strengths to support their weaknesses.

yoruba: Nígbàtí ọwọ́ ò tí ì gbọ́n lojú ńṣepin.
english_literal: It is when the hands have not learned wisdom that the eyes ooze matter.
interpretation_gold: A wise person will know how to manage and conceal his shortcomings.
deepseek_translation: When the hand has not learned wisdom, the eye is the one suffering.
claude_translation: When the hand has not yet become wise, the eye closes.
gemini_translation: When the hand is not yet wise, the eye is blinking.
mistral_translation: When the hand does not have wisdom, it tears things apart in front of the eyes.
llama_translation: When the hand is not yet full, it is already counting the fingers.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb warns that lack of wisdom or experience leads to avoidable suffering or consequences.
claude_interpretation: Inexperience or lack of skill leads to failure or missed opportunities.
gemini_interpretation: This proverb suggests that inexperience or lack of skill often leads to hesitation or uncertainty.
mistral_interpretation: Lack of wisdom or foresight leads to self-destructive actions that are obvious to others.
llama_interpretation: One should not count on something until it is fully achieved.

yoruba: Nítorí-i ká lè ríbi gbé e la ṣe ńṣe ọyàn sódó.
english_literal: It is so that one would have a means of lifting it that one carves breasts [handles] on the mortar.
interpretation_gold: One should anticipate problems and prepare solutions for them.
deepseek_translation: Because we can carry it easily is why we make the load heavy.
claude_translation: It is so that we can see where to place it that we make a selection at the mortar
gemini_translation: It is so that we can have a place to put it that we make pounded yam in a mortar.
mistral_translation: So that we can find where to keep it, we are making a basket by the roadside
llama_translation: Because of the way we are, we are carrying the load on our heads to the market
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns against taking advantage of someone's kindness or willingness to help by burdening them excessively.
claude_interpretation: Careful observation and assessment should precede any important decision or action.
gemini_interpretation: One should prepare for future needs or consequences by creating the necessary provisions or conditions.
mistral_interpretation: One should prepare adequately for the future to avoid unnecessary struggles or losses.
llama_interpretation: One's circumstances or nature can lead to unnecessary struggles or hardships.

yoruba: “Níbo ló gbé wà?” nìyájú ẹkùn.
english_literal: “Where is it?” is a great insult to the leopard.
interpretation_gold: One should be smart enough to hide one's ignorance about things one should know.
deepseek_translation: "Where did it carry being?" in front of the leopard.
claude_translation: Where did it stay? is the shame of the leopard.
gemini_translation: “Where is it?” is the impatience of the leopard.
mistral_translation: Where did it live? is the lion's question.
llama_translation: Where did the leopard meet us?
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns against questioning the obvious or challenging those clearly more powerful.
claude_interpretation: A leopard's spotted pattern reveals everywhere it has been, teaching that one's actions and whereabouts cannot be hidden as they leave permanent marks or evidence.
gemini_interpretation: The proverb highlights that impatience is a characteristic trait of the leopard, implying that some individuals are naturally predisposed to being impatient.
mistral_interpretation: The proverb highlights the tendency of the powerful to question or dismiss the origins of those they perceive as weaker.
llama_interpretation: This proverb cautions against blaming others for one's own misfortunes or circumstances.

yoruba: Ní ìlú tí a ò ti fẹ́ ẹyẹlé, adìẹ yóò ṣọ̀wọ́n níbẹ̀.
english_literal: In a town that does not welcome pigeons, chickens will be very scarce there.
interpretation_gold: Onerous things will not be countenanced where easy obligations are not.
deepseek_translation: In a town where there are no pigeons, chickens will be used as sacrifices.
claude_translation: In a town where pigeons are not loved, chickens will be precious there.
gemini_translation: In a town where pigeons are not loved, chickens will be scarce there.
mistral_translation: In a town where one does not want the pigeon, the chicken will be scarce there.
llama_translation: In the town where we have not paid homage to the elephant, the chicken will make a lot of noise there.
deepseek_interpretation: When the preferred option is unavailable, people will make do with what they have.
claude_interpretation: When better options are not valued or available, lesser alternatives become highly prized.
gemini_interpretation: When people do not appreciate what is readily available or common, they will struggle to find even more valuable or desirable alternatives.
mistral_interpretation: When people reject what is good or valuable, they will end up with something worse or less desirable.
llama_interpretation: In a place where there is no strong authority or respect, the weak or insignificant will dominate.

yoruba: Nítorí adití lòjò fi ńṣú; nítorí afọ́jú ló ṣe ńkù.
english_literal: It is for the benefit of deaf people that rain clouds gather; it is for the benefit of the blind that thunder rumbles.
interpretation_gold: The wise person should be able to read portents and take precautions.
deepseek_translation: Because of the deaf, the rain falls; because of the blind, it drizzles.
claude_translation: Because of the deaf person, the rain continues to fall; because of the blind person, it continues to be dark.
gemini_translation: It is because of the deaf that the rain falls; it is because of the blind that it thunders.
mistral_translation: Because of the clear sky the rain falls; because of blindness it misses the target.
llama_translation: Because of the heat of the sun, it is used to dry; because of the cold of the night, it is used to chill.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb teaches that nature operates independently of human limitations or perceptions.
claude_interpretation: Problems persist when those responsible for solutions are unable or unwilling to address them due to their limitations or negligence.
gemini_interpretation: Events often have multiple causes or are perceived differently by individuals with varying abilities or perspectives.
mistral_interpretation: Misfortune or failure often results from unseen or overlooked factors, not just obvious circumstances.
llama_interpretation: Different circumstances require different approaches.

yoruba: Ohun tó ní òun óò bẹ́ni lórí, bó bá ṣíni ní fìlà, ká dúpẹ́.
english_literal: If a thing that vows to decapitate one only knocks off one's hat, one shounld be thankful.
interpretation_gold: If the misfortune that befalls one turns out to be far milder than one expected, one should give thanks.
deepseek_translation: Whatever says it will break your head, if it tears your cap, give thanks.
claude_translation: Something that says it will not touch one's head, if it makes one a cap, let us give thanks.
gemini_translation: That which says it will cut off one's head, if it only removes one's cap, let us be grateful.
mistral_translation: The thing that says it will cut itself on the head, if it lands on a cap, let us give thanks
llama_translation: Something that has its owner on top, if it falls, it falls on its back
deepseek_interpretation: Be grateful for minor misfortunes as they could have been worse.
claude_interpretation: We should be grateful when something we feared would harm us instead brings us benefit or honor.
gemini_interpretation: It is wise to be grateful when a potential disaster turns out to be less severe than anticipated.
mistral_interpretation: When a misfortune narrowly avoids causing greater harm, one should be grateful for the lesser outcome
llama_interpretation: A person who is well-prepared and in control will be able to handle challenges with ease.

yoruba: Olòṣì ọmọ ní ńfọwọ́ òṣì júwe ilé-e baba-a ẹ̀.
english_literal: It is a worthless child that points the way to his father's house with his left-hand fingers.
interpretation_gold: One should show proper regard for one's own patrimony.
deepseek_translation: The poor child is the one who points to the father's house with the left hand.
claude_translation: It is a poor child that uses the left hand to point to his father's house
gemini_translation: A poor child uses a poor hand to point to his father's house.
mistral_translation: A poor man's child describes his father's house by pointing at the poor man's house
llama_translation: The child of a lazy person is the one who cleans the father's house
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb teaches that one should not disrespect or neglect their family, especially in times of need.
claude_interpretation: One should not speak badly of or disrespect their own family or origins, as it reflects poorly on themselves.
gemini_interpretation: One's current circumstances or appearance should not be used to judge or diminish their noble origins or heritage.
mistral_interpretation: Children often reflect or inherit the social and economic status of their parents, highlighting the cycle of poverty or privilege.
llama_interpretation: A person's laziness can lead to their children suffering the consequences.

yoruba: Owó tọ́mọdé bá kọ́kọ́ ní, àkàrà ní ńfi-í rà.
english_literal: The first money a youth comes into he spends on bean fritters.
interpretation_gold: The youth seldom know how to manage their wealth.
deepseek_translation: The money a child gathers with a basket, is what they use to buy bean cakes.
claude_translation: The money a child first learns to count with, they use it to buy bean cakes.
gemini_translation: The money a child first earns, he uses it to buy akara.
mistral_translation: The money a child gathers in the morning, he spends on bean cakes.
llama_translation: The money that a child has, it is with corn cake that it is being spent.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb teaches that one should make do with what they have, no matter how little.
claude_interpretation: People tend to spend their first earnings or money on simple, immediate pleasures rather than saving or investing wisely.
gemini_interpretation: Children often spend their first earnings on simple pleasures or immediate gratification.
mistral_interpretation: A person who earns money easily or prematurely often wastes it on frivolous things.
llama_interpretation: A person's wealth is often squandered on trivial things.

yoruba: Oko kì í jẹ́ ti baba àti tọmọ kó má nìí àlà.
english_literal: Farms do not, by virtue of belonging to a father and his son, lack boundaries.
interpretation_gold: Even close relatives may benefit from good fences.
deepseek_translation: A farm does not belong to both father and child without having a boundary.
claude_translation: A farm does not belong to both father and child without there being a boundary mark.
gemini_translation: A farm does not belong to both father and son without having boundaries.
mistral_translation: The farm does not prevent a father and his child from having the same dream.
llama_translation: A farm does not spoil at the father's and the child's place
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb emphasizes the importance of clear boundaries and individual ownership, even among family members.
claude_interpretation: Even in close family relationships, clear boundaries and defined ownership must be established to prevent conflicts.
gemini_interpretation: Even within close relationships, clear boundaries and divisions of responsibility are necessary to prevent conflict and maintain order.
mistral_interpretation: Shared experiences or challenges do not erase the natural bond and similarities between parent and child.
llama_interpretation: A family's reputation is preserved when both parents and children behave responsibly.

yoruba: Owó kì í lóye kọ́mọ kú sẹ́rú.
english_literal: If the amount of money is known, a child cannot die in slavery.
interpretation_gold: One does not endure adverse conditions when one is capable of the effort to escape them.
deepseek_translation: Money does not buy sense for a child to avoid becoming a slave.
claude_translation: Money does not have sense to teach a child to die as a slave
gemini_translation: Money does not have the wisdom to teach a child to die as a slave.
mistral_translation: Money does not have understanding to bury a child as a slave
llama_translation: Money does not go to the market to buy a child's corpse.
deepseek_interpretation: Wealth alone cannot prevent foolishness or its consequences.
claude_interpretation: Wealth without wisdom can lead to the destruction of future generations through poor decisions and lack of proper guidance.
gemini_interpretation: Wealth cannot buy wisdom or prevent a person from making foolish and self-destructive choices.
mistral_interpretation: Wealth cannot replace the value of a child or compensate for their loss
llama_interpretation: One should not spend money on a lost cause or a hopeless situation.

yoruba: O kò wọ bàtà nínù ẹ̀gún ò ńsáré; o lágbára màlúù?
english_literal: You have no shoes on on the thorny path and yet you are running; do you have a cow's “hoof” power?
interpretation_gold: Unless one is well fortified one should not court danger.
deepseek_translation: He who does not wear shoes in the thorns is running; are you stronger than a cow?
claude_translation: He doesn't wear shoes in thorns and he's not running; does he have the strength of a bull?
gemini_translation: You don't wear shoes in thorns and you are running; do you have the strength of a cow?
mistral_translation: You do not wear shoes while the thorn is running; do you have the strength of a cow?
llama_translation: He doesn't wear shoes inside the masquerade's house, yet he's boasting of strength
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb warns against reckless behavior by highlighting that even the strong (like a cow) avoid unnecessary harm.
claude_interpretation: This questions someone who acts carelessly or recklessly without proper preparation, asking if they think they are invincible.
gemini_interpretation: It is foolish to engage in a difficult or dangerous task without proper preparation or protection, as it suggests an unrealistic overestimation of one's own capabilities.
mistral_interpretation: It is foolish to ignore obvious dangers or fail to prepare adequately for challenges.
llama_interpretation: One should not boast of abilities they have not demonstrated in a challenging situation.

yoruba: Okotorobo-ó yé ẹyin sílẹ̀, àdàbà ńgarùn wo ẹyin ẹlẹ́yin.
english_literal: Okotorobo the bird lays an egg, and the turtle dove stretches its neck to inspect the egg that does not belong to it.
interpretation_gold: One should mind one's own business.
deepseek_translation: The hawk abandons the eggs, the dove comes to inspect the eggs of the hen.
claude_translation: The okotorobo bird has laid eggs on the ground, the dove is looking longingly at another's eggs.
gemini_translation: The Okotorobo bird lays its eggs on the ground, the dove watches the eggs of the egg-layer.
mistral_translation: The one-legged person does not abandon eggs, the dove is counting the eggs of the egg-seller
llama_translation: The tortoise's mother is on the ground, the lizard's mother is on the wall.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb warns against neglecting one's responsibilities, as others may take advantage of the situation.
claude_interpretation: People often desire what others have while neglecting or undervaluing their own possessions.
gemini_interpretation: This proverb highlights the irony of someone neglecting their own responsibilities while being overly concerned with or observing the affairs of others.
mistral_interpretation: Do not neglect your responsibilities or possessions, as others may be monitoring or waiting to take advantage of your negligence.
llama_interpretation: This proverb highlights the differences in people's circumstances and backgrounds.

yoruba: O fi awọ ẹkùn ṣẹbọ àìkú; ẹkùn ìbá má kùú ìwọ ìbá rawọ ẹ̀ ṣoògùn?
english_literal: You use a leopard's skin as an ingredient for medicine to hold off death; had the leopard not died would you have had access to its hide for the medicine?
interpretation_gold: One should not chase impossible dreams.
deepseek_translation: He used the skin of a leopard for sacrifice to avoid death; if the leopard were alive, would you dare rub its body for medicine?
claude_translation: He used leopard's skin to make medicine against death; if leopards don't die, would you buy their skin for medicine?
gemini_translation: You used the skin of a leopard to make a charm for immortality; if the leopard had not died, would you have been able to use its skin for medicine?
mistral_translation: You use a leopard's skin to offer sacrifice for immortality; if the leopard had not died, would you have gotten its skin to use as medicine?
llama_translation: He used the leopard's skin to deceive the death; will the leopard's skin not be torn when it sees the hunter?
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns against taking advantage of someone's weakness or absence, as they would not dare to do so if the person were present or strong.
claude_interpretation: It is illogical to trust something that contradicts itself or to believe in solutions that don't work for their own source.
gemini_interpretation: One cannot achieve a desired outcome without the necessary sacrifice or prerequisite event, even if that event is undesirable.
mistral_interpretation: One cannot achieve great things without the sacrifices or contributions of others.
llama_interpretation: One's deceitful actions will eventually be exposed when faced with the consequences.

yoruba: Ogún mbókòó? Òwe aṣiwèrè.
english_literal: Twenty or a score? An imbecile's puzzle.
interpretation_gold: Trust an imbecile to pose stupid questions.
deepseek_translation: Twenty is a hoe? A proverb of madness.
claude_translation: Is Ogun carrying a hoe? It's the proverb of a mad person.
gemini_translation: Is war coming? A proverb of a madman.
mistral_translation: Twenty heads? A proverb of a madman.
llama_translation: Ogún is not a farmer? It is a proverb.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb criticizes nonsensical or illogical statements, implying they are as absurd as calling a number a farming tool.
claude_interpretation: It is foolish to question whether the god of iron and farming would carry the very tool he represents and governs.
gemini_interpretation: It is foolish to anticipate or provoke conflict unnecessarily.
mistral_interpretation: It mocks someone who overcomplicates a simple matter, like a fool trying to count too many things at once.
llama_interpretation: This proverb highlights the importance of knowing one's limits and not pretending to be something one is not.

yoruba: Ojú tó rọ̀ nirorẹ́ ńsọ.
english_literal: Pimples attack only faces that are delicate.
interpretation_gold: People always take advantage of gentle people.
deepseek_translation: The eye that sees the farm is watering it.
claude_translation: The eye that sheds tears is the one that speaks kindness
gemini_translation: The eye that cries is the one that tells the story.
mistral_translation: The eye that cries will eventually dry up and heal.
llama_translation: The eye that sees tomorrow is the one that is awake
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb teaches that seeing potential or opportunity is the first step toward nurturing and achieving success.
claude_interpretation: Those who have experienced suffering or hardship are often the most compassionate and understanding toward others.
gemini_interpretation: Those who have experienced hardship are best positioned to recount its details and impact.
mistral_interpretation: Sorrow or hardship is temporary, and one will eventually recover from it.
llama_interpretation: Vigilance and preparedness are necessary for a successful future.

yoruba: Orín yí, ìlù-ú yí padà.
english_literal: The song changes, and the drumming changes to suit.
interpretation_gold: One should match one's behavior to one's circumstances.
deepseek_translation: The song changes, the drum changes.
claude_translation: This song, this drum has changed.
gemini_translation: The song changes, the drum changes.
mistral_translation: This song, this drumming has returned.
llama_translation: This song, the drumming of it is enough
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb signifies that situations and circumstances are constantly evolving, requiring adaptability.
claude_interpretation: The situation or circumstances have completely changed from what they used to be.
gemini_interpretation: Circumstances dictate a change in approach or response.
mistral_interpretation: A situation or event that was thought to be over has unexpectedly repeated itself.
llama_interpretation: One's actions or behavior can be sufficient to reveal one's true nature or intentions.

yoruba: “Ó ṣe mí rí”; ògbó adìẹ-ẹ́ rí àwòdì sá.
english_literal: “I have experienced it before”; a grown chicken flees at the sight of a kite.
interpretation_gold: One learns to run from danger once one has recognized it for what it is.
deepseek_translation: “It happened to me”; the old man saw the hawk and ran.
claude_translation: It has done me harm; the hen's elder saw the hawk and ran away
gemini_translation: “It happened to me”; the old hen saw the hawk and ran away.
mistral_translation: “You did it to me”; the old hen sees the hawk fleeing
llama_translation: He did me a favour; the hen sees the hawk's shadow
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns that past experiences should teach caution, as the old man fled upon seeing the hawk due to prior harm.
claude_interpretation: Experience teaches wisdom - those who have faced danger before know to avoid it when they see it coming again.
gemini_interpretation: Experience teaches wisdom, as even an old hen, having encountered danger before, knows to flee from a hawk.
mistral_interpretation: The proverb teaches that those with experience can recognize danger or deception even when others do not.
llama_interpretation: One's enemies can see the danger that one cannot see.

yoruba: Onígi ní ńfigi ẹ̀ dọ́pọ̀.
english_literal: It is the firewood seller who sets a low price for his wares.
interpretation_gold: People take their cue from the owner of a thing in placing a value on it.
deepseek_translation: The owner of the wood is the one who piles the wood.
claude_translation: The owner of the stick is the one using his stick to stir the soup
gemini_translation: The owner of the wood uses his wood to make a replacement.
mistral_translation: It is the owner of the log that is cutting it to size for the mortar.
llama_translation: The wall is leaning on the fence.
deepseek_interpretation: Only the person in charge has the authority to make decisions or take action.
claude_interpretation: Only the person who owns or controls something has the right to decide how it should be used.
gemini_interpretation: People are responsible for replacing what they have lost or used up.
mistral_interpretation: One should take responsibility for their own problems and not expect others to solve them.
llama_interpretation: One who is weak or vulnerable often relies on someone or something stronger for support.

yoruba: Okotorobo-ó tùyẹ́ sílẹ̀ ọmọ titún ńgbe jó; ó ní ó rọ òun lọ́rùn lòún tu ú?
english_literal: Okotorobo, a bird, casts away a feather, and a young chick picks it up to dance with it; the one who shed the feathers asks, would I have discarded it if it was not a nuisance.
interpretation_gold: One should be careful before taking over things that others have rejected.
deepseek_translation: The old grasshopper jumps aside for the new grasshopper to dance; does it say it is lighter than it?
claude_translation: The okotorobo bird drops its feathers to the ground and a new chick picks them up to dance; it asks 'did it grow these feathers on its own neck before plucking them?'
gemini_translation: The Okotorobo bird defecated on the ground, and the newborn child picked it up to play; it said, 'Did it make my neck comfortable that I should pick it up?'
mistral_translation: The hunchback spreads a mat for the newborn to dance on; he asks if it is easy for him to spread it?
llama_translation: The tortoise that has a child on its back is dancing; it says it is the child that is dancing on its back
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb teaches humility and respect for elders, emphasizing that stepping aside for the younger generation does not diminish one's worth.
claude_interpretation: People should not take credit for or boast about things they did not create or earn themselves.
gemini_interpretation: This proverb highlights the innocence and lack of discernment in children, who may engage with things without understanding their true nature or implications.
mistral_interpretation: The proverb criticizes those who create difficulties for others yet complain about the effort it takes to do so.
llama_interpretation: This proverb highlights the tendency for people to shift blame or responsibility to others, often to avoid accountability.

yoruba: Owú pani ju kùm̀mọ̀.
english_literal: Jealousy kills more surely than a cudgel.
interpretation_gold: Jealousy is a dangerous thing.
deepseek_translation: Hunger kills more than poison.
claude_translation: Cotton kills more than a club.
gemini_translation: Jealousy kills more than a club.
mistral_translation: Cotton kills more than a knife.
llama_translation: A dead person is better than a mute person.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb emphasizes that the suffering caused by hunger is more severe and deadly than that caused by poison.
claude_interpretation: Soft, gentle things can be more dangerous or harmful than obviously threatening ones.
gemini_interpretation: Jealousy is a destructive emotion that can cause more harm than physical violence.
mistral_interpretation: Seemingly harmless things can cause greater harm than obvious dangers.
llama_interpretation: It is better to be gone than to be present but unable to express oneself or contribute to a situation.

yoruba: Olóhun kì í rí ohun ẹ̀ kó pè é lórò.
english_literal: The owner will not see what he owns and call it a fearful; abomination.
interpretation_gold: One cannot be fearful of what one owns.
deepseek_translation: God does not see something and call it a mystery.
claude_translation: God does not see something and call it expensive.
gemini_translation: The owner does not see his property and call it a taboo.
mistral_translation: God does not see a thing and delay in punishing it as wrongdoing
llama_translation: The deaf does not hear the thing that is called by its name
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb means that nothing is beyond God's understanding or control.
claude_interpretation: Nothing is too costly or difficult for God to provide or accomplish.
gemini_interpretation: People do not speak ill of or condemn what belongs to them or what they value.
mistral_interpretation: Divine justice is certain and will not be delayed for any wrongdoing
llama_interpretation: One who is unwilling to listen or pay attention will not understand or respond to a message, no matter how clearly it is communicated.

yoruba: Olóhun-ún dolè; “Gbà bù jẹ́” dolóhun.
english_literal: The owner becomes a thief; “Take this and eat” becomes the owner.
interpretation_gold: The tables are turned, such that the rightful owner is displaced by a usurper.
deepseek_translation: God owns the house; 'Accept and endure' owns God.
claude_translation: The creditor becomes the debtor; 'Take and eat' becomes the creditor.
gemini_translation: The owner became lazy; 'Take and eat' became the owner.
mistral_translation: God owns the house; 'Please, let me have it' owns God.
llama_translation: The one who has a secret is at home; 'Take and eat' is the secret.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb teaches that patience and endurance are divine virtues favored by God.
claude_interpretation: Roles and circumstances can reverse unexpectedly, where the one who was owed becomes the one who owes.
gemini_interpretation: Negligence and inaction can lead to the loss of one's possessions or authority to those who are more proactive.
mistral_interpretation: The proverb highlights the power of polite and humble requests in overcoming even divine authority.
llama_interpretation: This proverb cautions against revealing confidential information, as it can lead to trouble.

yoruba: Orí ọ̀kẹ́rẹ́ popo láwo; bí a wí fọ́mọ ẹni a gbọ́ràn.
english_literal: The squirrel's head sits in a plate like a lump; if one counsels one's child it should listen.
interpretation_gold: Refusal to listen to counsel leads to disaster.
deepseek_translation: The head of the stranger is big like a pot; if we mention our child's name, we listen.
claude_translation: The head of a squirrel is completely bald; when one speaks to one's child, one listens to advice.
gemini_translation: The head of the distant one is bald; if we speak to our child, they will obey.
mistral_translation: The head of a squirrel is full of lines like a woven mat; if we speak in parables, our children will understand advice
llama_translation: The head of the okere tree is big on the outside; when you peel it, you will see the smallness of its content.
deepseek_interpretation: People often pay more attention to outsiders than their own family members.
claude_interpretation: Just as a squirrel's bald head is obvious to all, when you counsel your child, you should also be open to receiving wisdom in return.
gemini_interpretation: This proverb suggests that while outsiders may be difficult to influence, one's own children are expected to be receptive to guidance and instruction.
mistral_interpretation: Using simple, relatable examples makes wisdom easier to grasp and remember for future generations
llama_interpretation: Appearance can be deceiving, and true worth is often hidden beneath the surface.

yoruba: Ojú kì í pọ́nni ká mu ìṣápá; òùngbẹ kì í gbẹni ká mu ẹ̀jẹ̀.
english_literal: One is never so desperate that one drinks red sorrel juice; one is never so thirsty that one drinks blood.
interpretation_gold: Desperation must never push one beyond the bounds of acceptable behavior.
deepseek_translation: The eye does not hurt someone and then make them take a staff; the mouth does not offend someone and then make them take a knife.
claude_translation: Eyes do not deceive one to drink palm wine; thirst does not dry one up to drink blood
gemini_translation: The eye does not become red (inflamed) and one drinks sorrel; one does not become thirsty and drink blood.
mistral_translation: The eye does not become swollen so that we can drink bean soup; the throat does not become hoarse so that we can drink blood
llama_translation: The eye does not go to sleep and the eyelid does; the ear does not go to sleep and the earring does.
deepseek_interpretation: One's actions or words should not provoke others to retaliate with violence.
claude_interpretation: One should not use circumstances as an excuse to engage in forbidden or harmful actions.
gemini_interpretation: One should not resort to inappropriate or harmful solutions when faced with a problem.
mistral_interpretation: People do not endure suffering or hardship just to satisfy the desires or whims of others
llama_interpretation: One part of a whole cannot function independently without the other.

yoruba: Oòrùn kì í jẹ iṣu àgbà kó má mọbẹ̀.
english_literal: An elder does not lose his yams to the sun without knowing where the event happened.
interpretation_gold: A grown up person should know where he went wrong and make amends accordingly.
deepseek_translation: The sun does not eat an old yam without knowing its place.
claude_translation: The sun does not eat an elder's yam without knowing how to peel it
gemini_translation: The sun does not burn an elder's yam without it knowing the soup.
mistral_translation: The sun does not eat an elder's yam without adding salt to it
llama_translation: The sky does not eat the yam of the elder and then forget
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb means that experience and wisdom come with age, and elders should be respected for their knowledge.
claude_interpretation: One should not attempt tasks or claim privileges without having the necessary knowledge, skills, or wisdom to handle them properly.
gemini_interpretation: An elder's experience and wisdom allow them to anticipate and prepare for challenges.
mistral_interpretation: Respect for elders ensures their wisdom and contributions are properly valued and preserved
llama_interpretation: One should not forget the favors or kindness received from elders or those in positions of authority.

yoruba: Òjòwú ò lẹ́ran láyà.
english_literal: The jealous woman lacks flesh on her chest.
interpretation_gold: Excessive jealousy eats up the jealous.
deepseek_translation: The rain does not listen to the goat.
claude_translation: The coward has no courage in his heart.
gemini_translation: A jealous person has no meat in their chest.
mistral_translation: A jealous rain does not wet the meat in the open.
llama_translation: The rain does not wet the inside of the belly
deepseek_interpretation: Nature's forces do not heed the complaints or desires of individuals.
claude_interpretation: A person who lacks bravery cannot find inner strength when faced with challenges.
gemini_interpretation: Jealousy is a destructive emotion that consumes the jealous person from within, leaving them with nothing of value.
mistral_interpretation: Jealousy or ill-will from others cannot harm you if you are honest and transparent in your actions.
llama_interpretation: One's problems or troubles are not always visible to others.

yoruba: O ní kí ará ọ̀run ṣe oore fún ọ; bẹ́ẹ̀ni o rí ẹni tí eégún ńlé, tó fá lọ́bẹ̀ lá.
english_literal: You pray to the being from heaven to grant you a boon; yet you can see the person being chased by the masquerader and whose stew the masquerader has consumed.
interpretation_gold: One should not expect to receive better treatment from a person who is known to be vicious to others.
deepseek_translation: He said the people of heaven should do you good; did you see the person the masquerade is chasing, that he took to the farm?
claude_translation: He says the heavenly beings should do you a favor; likewise you see someone being chased by masquerades who draws a knife to cut through.
gemini_translation: He says that the people of heaven should do good for you; yet you see someone being chased by a masquerade, and he is licking soup.
mistral_translation: He said the heavenly beings should do you a favor; meanwhile, you see the person the masquerade is visiting, who has taken away the knife.
llama_translation: He said the people of heaven should make a road for him; but when he got there, he saw someone whose load was heavier, and he was carrying it on his head.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns against relying on divine intervention without taking practical action to address one's problems.
claude_interpretation: When seeking divine intervention or help, one must also be prepared to take decisive action to solve their own problems.
gemini_interpretation: This proverb highlights the irony and foolishness of seeking blessings from distant sources while ignoring immediate dangers or opportunities.
mistral_interpretation: Do not ignore immediate help from those around you while waiting for distant or unlikely assistance.
llama_interpretation: One's problems are relative and may be less burdensome compared to others.

yoruba: Olówó á wá; aláwìn á wá; ìlú tí à ńgbé la gbé ńgbàwìn; à-rà-àì-san ni ò súnwọ̀n.
english_literal: Those who have money will come, and those who will buy on credit will come; it is in one's town that one buys on credit; failure to eventually pay up is what is bad.
interpretation_gold: There is nothing bad about buying on credit, as long as one eventually pays.
deepseek_translation: The wealthy will come; the poor will come; the town we live in we live in poverty; owing debts is not good.
claude_translation: The wealthy will come; the indebted will come; it is in the town where we live that we seek credit; buying without paying is not proper.
gemini_translation: The rich will come; the debtor will come; it is in the town where we live that we borrow; it is not paying back that is bad.
mistral_translation: The rich will come; the poor will come; the town we live in is where we spend our time; the one who buys on credit does not sleep soundly.
llama_translation: Money is coming; beauty is coming; the town where we live is the one we will take to heaven; it is the one we will not leave behind.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns against living beyond one's means and the consequences of accumulating debt.
claude_interpretation: It is acceptable to seek credit within your own community, but one must always honor their debts and pay what is owed.
gemini_interpretation: Borrowing is a natural part of community life, but failing to repay debts is unacceptable.
mistral_interpretation: Regardless of wealth or status, everyone faces their own struggles, and debt brings constant worry.
llama_interpretation: One's community and heritage are more valuable than material wealth or physical appearance.

yoruba: Òwú kì í là kínú bí olóko.
english_literal: The cotton seed does not open and thus anger the farmer.
interpretation_gold: The success of one's venture does not make one angry.
deepseek_translation: Cotton does not tear in the mouth like cornmeal.
claude_translation: Cotton does not spread out in the farm like the farmer.
gemini_translation: Cotton does not burst open in the heart like the farmer.
mistral_translation: Cotton does not tear inside like the farmer's wife
llama_translation: The death of a slave does not affect the farmer
deepseek_interpretation: Different things require different approaches or treatments.
claude_interpretation: A person should not overstep their boundaries or act beyond their proper role and status.
gemini_interpretation: The proverb highlights that while a farmer's heart may be burdened with worries about their crops, the cotton itself does not share or express such anxieties.
mistral_interpretation: Outsiders should not interfere in a household's internal conflicts or private matters.
llama_interpretation: The loss of a subordinate or someone of lower status does not significantly impact the person of higher status or authority.

yoruba: “Ó ḿbọ̀, ó ḿbọ̀!” la fi ńdẹ́rù ba ọmọdé; bó bá dé tán ẹ̀rù a tán.
english_literal: “It's coming! It's coming!” is what one says to frighten a child; after it has arrived it loses all its terror.
interpretation_gold: Looming problems often cause consternation out of all proportion to their real damaging force.
deepseek_translation: “It is heavy, it is heavy!” is how we carry a child; when it is time to put down, we put down.
claude_translation: It's coming, it's coming! is what we use to frighten children; when it arrives completely, the fear disappears.
gemini_translation: “It’s coming, it’s coming!” is how we scare a child; when it has arrived, the fear ends.
mistral_translation: “It is coming, it is coming!” is how we use to deceive a child; when it finally arrives, the load is gone.
llama_translation: “It is a lion, it is a lion!” is what is used to deceive a child; when it gets there, it is just a goat.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb teaches that responsibilities, though burdensome, are temporary and should be handled with care until they are no longer needed.
claude_interpretation: Empty threats lose their power once people realize there are no real consequences behind them.
gemini_interpretation: Anticipation of a threat can be more frightening than the actual event, which often proves less daunting than imagined.
mistral_interpretation: The proverb warns against empty promises or false assurances that lead to disappointment when expectations are not met.
llama_interpretation: This proverb warns against exaggeration or false pretenses, which can lead to disappointment or disillusionment.

yoruba: Ohun tí kò jẹ́ káṣọ pé méjì ni ò jẹ́ kó dú.
english_literal: The same thing that keeps one from having more than one item of clothing also keeps that one from blackening from dirt.
interpretation_gold: Misfortune teaches one fortitude; scarcity teaches one to be thrifty.
deepseek_translation: What does not allow the cloth to be two does not allow it to be torn.
claude_translation: What does not allow one to count two does not allow one to count three
gemini_translation: What prevents a cloth from being two is what prevents it from being black.
mistral_translation: What is not enough to make two garments is not enough to make even one
llama_translation: What does not eat two things is what we eat to be satisfied
deepseek_interpretation: Unity and togetherness prevent destruction and conflict.
claude_interpretation: If you cannot handle small responsibilities or tasks, you cannot handle bigger ones.
gemini_interpretation: A single, underlying cause often explains multiple related problems or deficiencies.
mistral_interpretation: If resources are insufficient for a complete or proper task, it is better not to attempt it at all
llama_interpretation: Moderation is key to satisfaction and contentment.

yoruba: “Òkè ìhín ò jẹ́ ká rí tọ̀ún” ò ṣéé pa lówe nílé àna ẹni.
english_literal: “The nearer hill kept one from seeing the farther one” is not a proverb one uses in one's parents-in-law's home.
interpretation_gold: There are some obligations one cannot sidestep with flippant excuses.
deepseek_translation: The hill of ants does not allow one to see the valley.
claude_translation: The hill over there that prevents us from seeing beyond cannot be killed with proverbs in one's in-laws' house
gemini_translation: “The hill here prevents us from seeing the one over there” cannot be used as a proverb in one's in-laws' house.
mistral_translation: The hill behind does not prevent us from seeing the one in front; it should not be used as a proverb in one's own hometown
llama_translation: The hill of yam heaps does not prevent one from seeing the road to the farm of another person
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb warns that focusing too much on minor issues can prevent one from seeing the bigger picture or more important matters.
claude_interpretation: Some problems or obstacles cannot be solved through indirect speech or diplomacy, especially when you're in a delicate social position where you must be careful with your words.
gemini_interpretation: One should be careful about what they say in the presence of their in-laws, as certain statements might be misinterpreted or cause offense.
mistral_interpretation: One should not use familiar or local knowledge to boast or deceive those who already know the truth.
llama_interpretation: One's own success or abundance should not blind them to the struggles or needs of others.

yoruba: Orí tó kọ ẹrù, owó ní ńnáni.
english_literal: A head that refuses “to carry” loads will cost its owner some money.
interpretation_gold: It costs money to get others to do for one what one refuses to do for oneself.
deepseek_translation: The head that refuses to carry a load, money is what it will carry.
claude_translation: The head that refuses to carry load, money is what burns it.
gemini_translation: The head that carries a load is the one that earns money.
mistral_translation: A head that carries a load, money is what it seeks
llama_translation: The head that wears the cap of a slave, money is its owner
deepseek_interpretation: If you avoid responsibilities, you will face financial struggles.
claude_interpretation: Those who avoid hard work will find themselves spending money unnecessarily or suffering financial consequences.
gemini_interpretation: Hard work and effort are necessary to achieve success and gain rewards.
mistral_interpretation: One who bears responsibility naturally looks for financial reward or support to sustain their efforts.
llama_interpretation: Wealth and material possessions can enslave and control an individual.

yoruba: Ó ti ojú orun wá ó ńfọ ẹnà; ó ní “ẹ jẹ́ ká máa ji ní mẹ́mu-mẹ́mu.”
english_literal: He woke up from sleep and spoke in scrambled language; he said, “Let us wake it in moos.”
interpretation_gold: An ignorant person will always make stupid suggestions.
deepseek_translation: He came from the sky and was blowing the trumpet; he said, "Let us wake up gradually."
claude_translation: He came from the face of heaven and is washing his hands; he says 'let us wake up gently-gently.'
gemini_translation: He came from the land of dreams and is clearing the path; he says, 'Let's be stealing little by little.'
mistral_translation: The one who came from the sky is boasting about the path; he says, 'Let us wake up gently.'
llama_translation: He came from heaven and was crying; he said 'let us eat and be satisfied in abundance'.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb advises taking things slowly and carefully rather than rushing into actions.
claude_interpretation: Someone who has experienced divine favor or good fortune should approach life with humility and gentleness rather than arrogance.
gemini_interpretation: This proverb describes someone who, having just woken up and still disoriented, proposes a foolish or impractical idea, highlighting the absurdity of acting without full awareness or consideration.
